verses.text: Therefore seeing we have this ministry, even as we obtained mercy, we don’t faint.

But we have renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by the manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.
Even if our Good News is veiled, it is veiled in those who perish;
in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, that the light of the Good News of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should not dawn on them.
For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake;
seeing it is God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,”  who has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.
We are pressed on every side, yet not crushed; perplexed, yet not to despair;
pursued, yet not forsaken; struck down, yet not destroyed;
always carrying in the body the putting to death of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body.
For we who live are always delivered to death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus may be revealed in our mortal flesh.
So then death works in us, but life in you.
But having the same spirit of faith, according to that which is written, “I believed, and therefore I spoke.”  We also believe, and therefore also we speak;
knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus, and will present us with you.
For all things are for your sakes, that the grace, being multiplied through the many, may cause the thanksgiving to abound to the glory of God.
Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day.
For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory;
while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.

footnotes.content: When Paul says "we don't faint," he's speaking to something every weary servant knows—the temptation to give up when the work is harder than you thought. But grace is not just a ticket to heaven; it's daily bread for daily work. He'd tasted mercy himself on the Damascus road, and it changed how he carried the burden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Renounced the hidden things of shame"—Paul names a real temptation here, one ancient orators knew well: the art of crafty persuasion over honest truth. He chooses the slower path: letting your conscience before God do the work, trusting that truth commends itself even when it doesn't dazzle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's a hard mercy: the Gospel may be veiled to some, but that veil is not on the message—it's on those who are perishing. Paul doesn't blame himself for their blindness. This freed him to proclaim boldly without needing to manage every hearer's response.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The blindness Paul speaks of is active, not accidental. He calls it what it is: a spiritual darkness that wars against light. Yet notice—he names Christ plainly: the image of God. Even in naming the enemy's work, Paul is proclaiming the One who breaks such darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We don't preach ourselves"—a whispered reproof to any servant who has caught themselves making a name. Paul's whole authority rests on one claim: Christ Jesus is Lord, and my job is to serve you toward Him, not away from Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul echoes Genesis 1:3—"Light will shine out of darkness." The same word that spoke creation into being now shines in a believer's heart. The face of Jesus Christ becomes the mirror where we see God's glory. It's not a cold doctrine; it's the warmth of knowing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Treasure in clay vessels." I've loved this verse for years—it's the antidote to spiritual pride. The power is not ours; we're just the carriers. When we crack and leak, that's not a failure; that's the treasure spilling through.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul pairs opposites: pressed but not crushed, perplexed but not despairing. He's not denying hardship; he's testifying to a grace that bends without breaking. There's always room to fall back, always a floor beneath the falling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Pursued, yet not forsaken." I hear a pastor who has run hard and looked back to find Jesus still there. "Struck down, yet not destroyed"—not because suffering ends, but because something in you stays alive when it should have been finished.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Carrying in the body the putting to death of Jesus"—Paul speaks of suffering as a kind of participation, a visible enactment of the crucifixion. But it's never for its own sake; the end is that His resurrection life becomes visible in us, too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Delivered to death for Jesus' sake"—Paul is describing a lifetime pattern, not a single crisis. And again, it's not morbid; it's the pathway by which His life becomes real to the Corinthians. Our surrender becomes His visibility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Death works in us, but life in you." What a trade. Paul is saying his sacrifice has fruit in the Corinthians' spiritual awakening. It's love made plain: I die so you live. And he says it without complaint, almost matter-of-factly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul quotes Psalm 116:10: "I believed, and therefore I spoke." He's rooting his courage in the Psalter, saying: the same faith that moved the psalmist moves us. Speech comes from belief; witness flows from trust. Silence is the only failure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here Paul plants his hope: the God who raised Jesus will raise us, too. He's not speaking theoretically; he's reminding the Corinthians that death is not the final word, and neither is suffering. The same power that turned the tomb inside out will keep its hand on you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul traces a beautiful chain: his suffering for them → their grace multiplies → thanksgiving abounds to God's glory. He sees all his hardship as a strand in a tapestry woven for praise. Nothing is wasted when God is at the loom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day." I've watched this happen in the elderly—the body slows, but something in them grows brighter. Paul knew it was real. The renewal isn't borrowed from tomorrow; it comes fresh each morning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Light affliction, which is for the moment." Paul's not minimizing real pain; he's sizing it against eternity. When you hold suffering in the palm of forever, it shrinks—not to nothing, but to something the glory outweighs. He's tasted that perspective and speaks from it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo here: in a world of surface noise and visible markers, Paul is pointing us toward the unseen—toward Jesus, toward eternal realities that the news cycle cannot touch. It's a whisper against the world's shouting. Looking back from 2026, how much of what seized our attention ten years ago has vanished, while the invisible things have only grown deeper?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
